description: This Attic red-figured amphora, dating from 480-460 BC, vividly depicts scenes from classical mythology, crafted with fine technique and traces of archaism. The obverse side illustrates "The Recognition of Theseus," where the youthful hero, presented beardless and adorned with a short undertied chiton, is grasped by Aegeus, an elderly man with white hair and a beard, who extends a rolled band. Aithra stands between them, elegantly dressed and touching Theseus' chin, while behind him is Pittheus, holding a trident, his figure expertly rendered but partially obscured by the design's border. The reverse side showcases a face-off between a similarly attired youth and Nike, who offers a phiale with grace and precision. The amphora exhibits refined details such as purple fillets and brown hair delineations, with the design encased within panels featuring key, lotus, and net patterns, enriched by a band of black rays around its body. Discovered in Vulci, this pottery piece not only embodies the rich artistic traditions of ancient Greece but also resonates with the enduring narratives of figures like Theseus, Aithra, Pittheus, Nike, and Aegeus.

This Attic black-figured amphora, dating from circa 510-500 BCE, exemplifies the artistry of Archaic Greek pottery. The amphora, crafted from pottery and skillfully painted and incised, vividly portrays a mythological narrative. Side (a) depicts Heracles wrestling Antaios, a dynamic scene where Heracles, nude and bearded, grapples with Antaios, who is also nude and bearded, his hand touching the earth. Above Heracles, a lion's skin, bow, quiver, and sword are suspended, signifying his legendary strength. Athena, adorned in a long embroidered chiton and aegis, stands to the left holding a spear and helmet, symbolizing divine intervention. Hermes appears on the right, bearded and dressed in a chiton and chlamys, pointing with his caduceus. An imitation inscription is inscribed above this scene. Side (b) illustrates the departure of a warrior in a quadriga, front-facing with a charioteer, a warrior, and accompanying animal motifs—a dog leaping and a bird descending. A merchant's mark under the foot features a lambda-eta ligature and deltoid mark, indicating its commercial use. Excavated from Vulci, this artifact encapsulates the intersection of myth and daily life in Greek culture, depicting figures such as Heracles, Antaios, Athena, and Hermes in classical mythology.

This Attic red-figure askos, dating from 470-400 BCE, exemplifies the intricate pottery techniques of ancient Greece. Wheel-made from fine buff clay, the askos features a flat body with splaying sides and a convex top, a prominent spout with an everted rim, and a basket handle. The surface, adorned in the red-figure technique on the shoulder, bears a patina of historical wear with certain portions of the black gloss now worn. On one side, a charming depiction of a beardless satyr on all fours with a bald crown is crafted facing the spout, while the opposite side showcases a bull with schematic detail and pronounced hooves, both figures directed toward the spout. Notably, the underside is marked with a single incised Cypriot syllabic character, offering a glimpse into cross-cultural influences. The artifact was unearthed at Marion-Arsinoe, underscoring its historical provenance within the realm of Greek antiquity.

This artifact is a body sherd from an Attic black-figured pottery band-cup, dating approximately to 550-525 BCE, during the Archaic period of Greek history. Expertly crafted through painting and incision techniques, the sherd is composed of pottery material. The interior is glazed black, while the exterior showcases a striking black-figure decorative frieze. The imagery features a siren with outspread wings in a rightward stance, confronting a deer. Notably, one wing and the lower body of the siren are missing, but traces of added red remain on the wing and body. The deer’s representation is preserved with its head, neck highlighted with red, and one foreleg still visible. This piece was excavated from the Sanctuary of Apollo at Naukratis, a site of significant religious and cultural activity in ancient Greece, offering a glimpse into the artistic and symbolic motifs of the Attic civilization.

This East Greek, Archaic Greek chalice fragment, dating approximately from 570-560 BCE, showcases the Chian Simple Animal Style, indicative of the period's artistic conventions. Composed of pottery with a cream slip, the rim and body sherds have been mended from two distinct fragments. The interior of the chalice features a reserved band at the rim with a glazed streaky black area below, adorned with a lotus flower outlined in added white and a red center, complemented by two white bands. The exterior displays a narrow black band atop the rim, a decorative pattern of short diagonal strokes between pairs of dilute bands, and a painted sphinx, with remnants of a red-haired head and curlicue directed to the left. This artifact was excavated at the Sanctuary of Aphrodite in Naukratis, a site recorded by the Ashmolean Museum register, offering invaluable insights into the cultural and religious contexts of Archaic Greece.

This rim sherd is a fragment of a Chian Simple Animal Style pottery chalice, originating from the East Greek, Archaic Greek culture, and is dated circa 570-560 BCE. Crafted from pottery, the sherd features a white slip with intricate decorations on both its interior and exterior. The interior is adorned with a reserved band at the rim and a glazed section below, fired to a red hue. The exterior is marked by a band of dots between dilute lines at the rim, with a painted decoration beneath, potentially depicting a sphinx, as suggested by the remaining strands of hair to the left. Slipped and painted techniques were employed in its creation, showcasing the artistic motifs prevalent during the period. This artifact was unearthed at Naukratis, contributing valuable knowledge to the understanding of cross-cultural interactions in ancient Greece.

This Attic red-figured chous, dating to approximately 420 BCE, is a masterful representation of Greek pottery, crafted from painted ceramic. The scene depicts two youthful but bearded satyrs engaging in playful antics. Central to the imagery are two jugs on the ground; a bearded satyr on the right holds a purple wreath aloft, while another approaches from the left, crouched with one hand resting on his knee and the other outreaching towards the jugs. The satyrs, bald on the crown and adorned with white ivy wreaths, are depicted with beardless yet youthful visages. This piece exemplifies a graceful miniature style, with eyes rendered in profile and the panel encapsulated by egg moulding above and below, and bordered on each side by herringbone patterns. This exquisite artifact was uncovered at Fikellura grave 179, offering valuable insights into the artistic and cultural conventions of ancient Greece.

This artifact is a handle plate from an Attic black-figured pottery column-krater, dating circa 575-550 BC, representative of the Archaic Greek period. The plate, made from pottery, exhibits a glazed streaky black underside and features a stepped zigzag pattern along its outer edges. The top of the handle plate showcases a black-figure decoration depicting a bird or possibly a siren facing left, though the head is missing, adorned with added red detailing on the chest, wing, and tail. The application of painting and incision techniques reflects the distinctive artistic practices of the time. This piece was excavated in Naukratis, an important cultural and trading center of ancient Greece, offering insights into the interplay of Greek art and commerce.

This artifact is a concave lip and wall sherd from an Attic black-glazed pottery cup, classified as type C, dating from 525-475 BC, during the Archaic Greek period. The piece features a sharply offset lip both internally and externally, which is thickened at the rim and entirely covered in a glossy black glaze. An inscription, rendered in Greek as a post-firing graffito, is located on the lip, although it is partially preserved and believed to contain a three-dot punctuation. The inscription tentatively names the classical deity Apollo, suggesting the vessel's potential religious or cultural significance. This pottery fragment was excavated at Naukratis, providing valuable insight into the exchange and influence of Greek culture across regions.

This tondo and stem sherd originates from an Attic black-figured pottery vessel, likely a type A cup, crafted during the Archaic Greek period circa 550-530 BCE. The interior decoration features a black-figure depiction of a bird or siren facing right, with distinct characteristics such as the body, outspread wings, one leg, and added red on the wing bands. A series of faded white dots adorns the underbelly, suggesting intricate detailing. The vessel's exterior displays a red fillet joining the bowl and stem, while the stem itself is glazed both inside and out. The underside is reserved with a red band at the top of the stem, accentuating its form. Composed of pottery and showcasing the painted and incised technique characteristic of the Attic style, this fragment offers insight into the artistic traditions of the time. It was possibly excavated at the ancient site of Naukratis, underlining its historical significance within Greek material culture.

This rim sherd of an Attic black-figured Type A cup, dating from around 525-500 BC, exemplifies the sophisticated artistry of Archaic Greek pottery. Crafted from pottery and employing both painted and incised techniques, this artifact features a striking black-figure exterior decoration, with a double ivy leaf frieze above a depiction of Dionysos, the classical deity. The rim's interior displays a reserved band, with the glaze fired to a reddish hue below. The representation of Dionysos shows his upper body cloaked, holding a horn, and likely extending a vine tendril. The field is further adorned with vine motifs, emphasizing the god's association with wine and revelry. This piece was excavated in Naukratis, a significant Greek trading post in Egypt, highlighting the cultural exchange between Greece and Egypt during this period.

This Archaic Greek hydria, dating to 500 BC, is a prime example of Attic pottery, characterized by its black-figure design set against a red panel backdrop, accentuated with purple and white accessories. The artwork features a striking depiction of divine and mythical figures: on the left, Dionysos is portrayed moving rightward, adorned with long hair, a beard, an ivy wreath, and wearing a long white chiton and himation. At the center, Apollo Citharoedos appears beardless with a laurel wreath, elegantly strumming a chelys using a plectrum, while drapery hangs from the instrument. Flanking Apollo are two suggested Maenads, clad in decorative chitons and himatia, indicative of their role as followers of Dionysos. Completing the scene on the right is Hermes, rendered with a backward glance, dressed in a short white chiton, chlamys, petasos, and endromides, and holding his iconic caduceus. The scene is intricately enhanced by a double honeysuckle motif above and bordered by a network pattern along the sides. This hydria was unearthed in Nola and exemplifies the artistry and mythological storytelling central to Greek ceramic work of the time.

This exquisite black-figured hydria, crafted around 520 BC during the Archaic Greek period, exemplifies Attic pottery through its intricate design and skilled craftsmanship. The vase is adorned with black designs set against a red panel, featuring accents in white and purple, and bordered by ivy motifs. On the shoulder of the hydria, a possible depiction of the mythological contest between Achilles and Memnon is presented, where the central figure, possibly Antilochus, lies flat and nude, while the armed warriors confront each other with spears and Boeotian shields, under the gaze of four spectating males holding wands. The main body showcases a marriage procession, highlighted by a quadriga carrying a male and female figure, both robed in opulent chiton and himation, accompanied by figures playing music and applauding. Inscribed with "Λυσιππίδης καλός, Ρόδον καλέ," the piece also bears a frieze of animals below, featuring a siren flanked by a panther and a doe. This hydria was uncovered in Vulci, an Etruscan city known for its rich archaeological findings, enhancing our understanding of ancient Greek iconography and cultural interactions.

This exquisite Attic red-figured hydria, dating to around 390 BC, exemplifies the ornate style of Greek pottery with its elaborate design painted on a black background. Adorned with white accessories, the vessel features intricate decorations such as egg-moulding around the lip and a maeander and chequer pattern below the primary scene. The central artwork depicts a dynamic tableau with a chariot drawn by two Erotes, ceremonially adorned and steering the vessel with Demeter and likely Core (Persephone) as passengers. These revered figures are portrayed with radiated fillets, ornate chitons, and intricate jewelry. Dancing Maenads, Satyrs, and seated figures populate the scene, each painstakingly detailed with beaded ornaments, necklaces, and embroidered garments. Iconographic elements include thyrsoi, tympana, and floral motifs, all indicating a celebration of the divine and mythical. The presence of notable deities such as Aphrodite and representations of Eros further infuse the piece with significant mythological narrative. This hydria was discovered in the Blacas Tomb, shedding light on burial practices and the cultural interplay between art and mythology in classical Greece.

This Attic black-figured hydria, crafted from pottery between 490 and 460 BCE, is a striking example of ancient Greek artistry. The design, rendered in black on a red panel, is bordered by intricate maeanders, palmettes, and dotted borders, with white accents adding depth to the composition. The scene depicts Nike, the personification of victory, elegantly flying to the right. She gazes back, her hair adorned with a white sphendone, while her outspread wings emerge from her breast. Nike's long chiton exhibits white markings, and she extends a white taenia with her hands, gracefully heading towards an altar topped by a blazing fire. A branch is delicately painted in the field, enhancing the visual narrative. This hydria, employing both painted and incised techniques, was discovered in Kalavarda, highlighting its cultural and religious significance as part of the rich tapestry of Greek civilization.

This Attic black-figured pottery lebes gamikos body sherd, dating from around 575-560 BC, is a fine representation of Archaic Greek artistry. The artifact, crafted from pottery and employing both painting and incising techniques, depicts a detailed scene on its exterior. It features part of a fallen Amazon to the right, the figure intricately detailed with a belted long chiton and a scabbard adorned with added red. The Amazon's face is outlined, with an eye showing a distinctive cornea meeting the upper eyelid. A Boeotian shield with a red border supports the figure, complemented by a spear positioned point downward, and an evocative touch of red depicting blood on the lower chiton part. The scene also includes the left leg and foot of another Amazon dashing to the right, and to the right side, a chain of vertical lotus and palmette with red highlights. A wide border of dots and alternating bands in red and black frames the scene intricately. The artifact bears a Greek inscription "Λυκοπις" (Lykopis) applied pre-firing on the wall. This pottery piece was excavated at the Sanctuary of the Dioskouroi in Naukratis, providing insight into its ceremonial use and the cultural exchanges within this Greek locale.

This exquisite Attic red-figured pottery lid from a lekanis, crafted circa 440 BC, exemplifies the finest style of Greek ceramic artistry. Adorned with a broad frieze encircling the central handle, it features intricate designs such as purple fillets, inscriptions, and wreaths. Surrounding the handle is an egg pattern, while the lips are decorated with alternating sets of maeanders and chequer squares. The artwork portrays seven Muses organized into three distinct groups: a seated Muse with broken away name, Polyhymnia, known by her inscribed name ΠΟΛΥ.ΝΙΑ, holding a likely scroll, and Cleio, ΚΛΕΩ, depicted with flutes; adjacent are Euterpe, inscribed ΕΥΤΕΡΠΕ, and Thaleia, ΘΑΛΕΙΑ, holding a wreath; lastly, Erato, inscribed as . . . ΤΩ, addressing Calliope with a square box. The Muses are elegantly depicted in long Ionic chitons with looped hair, except for Thaleia, who wears a Doric chiton with cropped hair. This lid was excavated from Nola, offering a glimpse into the rich decorative traditions of ancient Greece and the veneration of classical deities in the artistic milieu.

This exquisite Attic pottery piece, a red-figured lekanis with a lid, hails from the classical Greek period, specifically dated between 370-350 BCE. The lekanis is adorned with a striking design in red and white against a black ground, featuring egg-moulding on the cover and palmettes on the body, a testament to its intricate craftsmanship. The painted scene on the cover depicts a lively toilet scene centered around Eros, the classical deity of love, rendered with white flesh, red wings with black markings, and curly hair, holding an embroidered taenia. This vivid portrayal includes a seated female figure with an unguent-box and a cista, as well as another female figure running with a cista and taenia, both of whom are elegantly dressed in bordered garments. A youth, draped in fabric, sits with a calathos, while above him are intricate details including an embroidered taenia, tendrils, and an alabastron. This artefact, with its mythological associations and dynamic composition, was excavated in Puglia, offering a glimpse into the sophisticated artistry and cultural narratives of ancient Greece.

This Attic black-figure lekythos, dating from 480-460 BC, exemplifies the pottery techniques prominent in ancient Greece, specifically within the cultural context of Athens. The lekythos is crafted from pottery, employing both painting and incision techniques, and is adorned in a rather coarse style. The central design portrays the classical deity Dionysos, identifiable by his ivy-wreath, donned in a long white chiton with a purple border and a himation. He is depicted holding a keras and branches with fruit. Flanking Dionysos are two female figures, each elegantly poised on a mule, their hair encased under a fillet and cloaked in a himation. Completing the scene are two Satyrs, each grasping a taenia, with the one on the right glancing backwards, adding to the dynamic composition of the piece. This lekythos was excavated in Athens, shedding light on the religious and mythological narratives intrinsic to Greek society during this period.

This is a body sherd from an Attic black-figured pottery lip-cup, dating from circa 550-530 BC, representative of the Archaic Greek period. Crafted in Greece, the sherd is composed of pottery and exhibits both painted and incised techniques. Its interior design features a black zone bordered by alternating red and black tongue friezes, separated by sets of four black lines. Within the tondo, there is a black-figure decoration that appears to depict two male figures and an Amazon, all facing right, with the Amazon likely turning back. Of the male figures, one bent leg and one greaved leg are discernible, while for the Amazon, a white leg encased in a red greave is preserved. The exterior is predominantly black except for a portion of the reserved band at the outer break. This artifact, reflecting classical mythological themes, was excavated at Naukratis, an important ancient Greek trading post, providing a glimpse into the artistic and cultural exchanges of the time.

This Attic red-figured neck-amphora, produced between 450-430 BC, presents a serene depiction of possibly Zeus, seated regally to the right. The god is characterized by his beard, long hair adorned with a fillet, and an attire consisting of a long-sleeved chiton and himation. He holds a sceptre topped with a flower, and a tall stele on a plinth is situated behind him to the left. The reverse side features an ephebos, or young man, draped in a mantle and fillet, standing to the left while leaning on a crutch staff, his hair neatly looped over his ears. The vase is noted for its drawing of a good period, though executed somewhat carelessly, and uses purple for the fillet and a lighter brown for the hair and beard's ends. Decorative motifs include a meander beneath scene (a) and a row of ivy leaves beneath scene (b). This painted pottery, unearthed in Nola, richly embodies the classical artistic style and iconography of ancient Greece, shedding light on the era's cultural and religious conventions.

This exquisite Attic neck-amphora, dating approximately from 470-450 BCE, embodies the artistry of red-figure pottery through its detailed depictions encircling the vessel. Crafted from pottery and painted with a strong style, the amphora's most prominent imagery features the mythological contest between Heracles and Apollo for the sacred tripod. Heracles, depicted as beardless and nude, is in dynamic motion, carrying the tripod over his left shoulder while brandishing his club at Apollo who advances to reclaim it. Apollo is portrayed with long hair tied back, dressed in a short chiton with a mantle over his arms. The scene is further animated by the inscribed Greek words ΑΛΚΙΜΑXΩΣ KAΛΩΣ EΠIXAPΟΣ, celebrating the beauty of Alkimachos and Epicharos. On the reverse side, a stark contrast is presented with the figure of a bald, elderly man wrapped in a mantle, holding a staff and gazing backward. Notable features include the use of purple for headdresses and inscriptions, brown markings for Heracles' whiskers, and the transitional detailing of the eyes. The amphora, said to originate from Nola, is bordered by a continuous band of maeander beneath the illustrations, demonstrating the classical deity theme prevalent in Greek art.

This exquisite Attic red-figured neck-amphora, crafted between 470 and 450 BCE, exemplifies the classical artistry of ancient Greece, discovered in Vulci. Made from pottery and adorned using the painted technique, the amphora vividly depicts two scenes elegant in their simplicity. On one side (a), the goddess Nike, draped in a long-sleeved chiton, himation, and saccos, gracefully moves to the right, raising a fluted phiale in her right hand, while a woman in a mantle-tied long chiton accompanies her, holding an alabastron, her hair adorned with a double-wound fillet. The reverse side (b) reveals a narrative of two youths; as they walk to the right, each clad in a mantle and fillet, the latter raises a cotyle in his right hand. The piece is characteristic of the late strong style, noted for its increasingly indifferent execution. The amphora's decoration is framed by a strip of maeander below each scene, a tongue pattern above, and a net pattern adorning the sides, forming a cohesive and visually striking panel.

This exquisite Ancient Egyptian artifact from the 18th Dynasty, dating circa 1476-1457 BC, is a gold finger-ring featuring a turquoise-green glazed composition scarab as its bezel. The scarab is intricately detailed on its back and is set in a gold mount, inscribed with the prenomen or throne name of the renowned Queen Hatshepsut, flanked by hieroglyphs that translate to "The Good Goddess Maatkare, may she live." The ring's construction boasts a hollow gold foil shank, cleverly folded around a wire, with an additional wire threaded through the scarab's piercing to enable its swiveling function. The skillfully applied techniques include glazing, piercing, and incising, reflecting the craftsmanship of the era. This artifact, discovered in Egypt, offers a glimpse into the opulent and symbolically rich adornments of Egyptian royalty.

This elliptical name-bead from the 18th Dynasty, dated circa 1390-1352 BC, exemplifies the intricate artistry of Ancient Egyptian craftsmanship. Created from a bichrome glazed composition, it features a striking white on blue finish. The bead is designed with a double piercing and a cord channel on the back, allowing it to be worn as an adornment. The front of the bead is adorned with a painted cartouche that holds the prenomen of Pharaoh Amenhotep III, accompanied by the epithet "Good God," rendered in hieroglyphic script. This inscription emphasizes the divine and regal nature of the pharaoh's persona during his reign. The bead was found in Egypt, serving as a testament to the enduring legacy of Amenhotep III within Egyptian history and art.

This necklace from ancient Egypt, dating to the period after 650 BCE during the 26th Dynasty, is a remarkable artifact consisting of numerous green-blue glazed composition rectangular beads or plaques. Each bead is intricately incised with hieroglyphs naming Psamtek, known as Psammetichus, and features two longitudinal perforations for stringing. The glazing and incised techniques used highlight the sophisticated craftsmanship of the era. The necklace, associated with Psamtek—a prominent figure of the 26th Dynasty—illuminates the cultural and artistic practices of ancient Egypt. Discovered in Egypt, this piece serves as a testament to the region's rich history and the enduring legacy of its pharaonic rulers.

This artifact is a glazed composition New Year's flask from the Late Period, specifically the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dating to approximately the 6th century BC. The flask, though partially preserved, displays intricate geometric designs such as tear drops and rectangles arranged in a broad collar of concentric registers on its upper body. A central vertical band features a hieroglyphic inscription, which is framed by vertical bands decorated with a scale pattern. The inscription, rendered in Egyptian hieroglyphics, translates to a traditional blessing: "May Amun-Ra inaugurate a perfect year." Crafted using a mould-made technique from a now glaze-lost greenish-yellow fine paste, this object reflects the cultural significance of Amun-Ra in New Year rituals. The flask was excavated at Naukratis, one of the key Greek trading hubs in Egypt, emphasizing its role in cultural exchanges of the period.

This exquisite 19th Dynasty Egyptian pectoral, dated circa 1275 BC, is a remarkable example of ancient artistry and religious symbolism. Crafted from glazed composition, it is shaped like a pylon, mimicking the monumental gateway entrances of Egyptian temples. The pectoral features sloping sides and a curved cavetto cornice, decorated with block patterns around its edges. Its vibrant color palette—yellow inlaid with blue, red, and green glazes—emulates precious materials like gold, lapis lazuli, cornelian, and turquoise. Central to the design is a dark blue heart scarab, representing lapis lazili and depicted within a solar barque, flanked by the goddesses Isis and Nephthys, whose hieroglyphic inscriptions label them as "Lady of the West" and "Mistress of the Necropolis." Additional protective symbols include a 'djed' pillar, the Girdle of Isis amulet, and two wedjat eyes, all intricately inlaid with polychrome glazes. On the pectoral's reverse, Chapter 30B from the 'Book of the Dead' is inscribed in turquoise green hieroglyphs, naming the deceased as Lady Ptahemheb. The underside also features a pattern of parallel dark blue lines forming a square frame around the scarab. Six holes are strategically placed for attachment to mummy wrappings, indicating its funerary use. Unearthed in historic Memphis, this pectoral highlights the convergence of artistry, religious devotion, and funerary practices in ancient Egypt.

This artifact is a mould-made scarab crafted from a glazed composition, dating from the 26th Dynasty of Egypt, approximately between 664 and 510 BC, plausibly during the reigns of Psamtek I or Apries. The scarab's back is simply modeled, featuring single lines delineating the prothorax and elytra, while the sides display highly simplified legs indicated by two horizontal grooves. Its underside is adorned with a hieroglyphic inscription, horizontally organized and deeply impressed, reading "wAH-ib-ra," which translates to "Wahibre (Constant [is the] Heart [of] Re)." This inscription may reference the prenomen of Psamtek I or the nomen of Apries. Pierced longitudinally, the scarab exhibits a dirty brown glaze, possibly yellow originally, with a hard, pale yellow core underneath. This piece, excavated from Naukratis, reflects the intricate religious and cultural symbolism prevalent during the period, serving both as an amulet and a testament to the artistry of the era.

This Ancient Egyptian scarab, dating from 600 to 570 BC, originates from the 26th Dynasty and is believed to have been crafted at the Scarab Factory. Made from a glazed composition using mold-made, incised, and pierced techniques, the scarab has endured significant erosion over the centuries. While the back is notably rubbed, the divisions for the head, prothorax, and elytra remain discernible. The scarab's underside, although badly worn, features an incised vertical line separating a possibly unidentified figure to the right and a partial cartouche to the left. This cartouche contains three debased hieroglyphic signs, potentially representing a cross-shaped symbol flanked by two discs. This symbol might be interpreted as a debased version of the Horus name of Psamtek I or the nomen of Apries, based on interpretations by Gorton. The scarab, with its light yellow paste and almost nonexistent glaze—whether due to erosion or absence—is longitudinally pierced, reflecting the intricate artistry and symbolic significance embedded in Egyptian craftsmanship and regal iconography.

This artifact is a mould-made scarab, dating from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, between 600 and 570 BC. Crafted with a glazed composition and adorned in a yellow glaze, the scarab's underside is inscribed with three horizontally arranged hieroglyphic signs: a Maat feather pointing to the right, followed by an owl and an ankh sign. The hieroglyphs may possess either magical significance or a cryptographic rendition of the divine name Amun. Such scarabs were common amulets in ancient Egyptian culture, often symbolizing rebirth and protection. This particular piece was excavated at Naukratis, a significant ancient Greek trading post in Egypt, illustrating the cultural exchanges in the region during this era.

This small mould-made scaraboid, dating from 600 to 570 BC during Egypt's 26th Dynasty, exemplifies ancient Egyptian craftsmanship in bright blue Egyptian paste. The back is simply modeled, with incised lines indicating the clypeus, prothorax, and elytra, and notches denoting humeral callosities. The legs are abstractly represented by broad incised lines forming a triangle. The underside bears three hieroglyphic inscriptions: the Maat feather, an owl, and a sun-disc, which cryptographically reference the divine name Amun. Noteworthy for its longitudinal piercing, this artifact bears cultural and religious significance potentially linked to Amun-Ra. Discovered in Naukratis, this scaraboid offers insight into the religious and artistic practices of the period.

This artifact is a mould-made scarab from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dating between 600 and 570 BC. Crafted from a glazed composition, the scarab's back is severely damaged, lacking detailed modeling, and only limited incised grooves suggestive of legs remain visible on its sides. The underside bears a poorly preserved hieroglyphic inscription, arranged horizontally from right to left, featuring the falcon, men-draughtboard sign, and sun-disc. This inscription might have been stamped rather than incised. The scarab is longitudinally pierced, though much of its glaze is lost, revealing a yellowish off-white core, now heavily worn. The inscription is possibly a cryptic way to denote Amun or Amun-Ra, or the Horus name of Psamtek II. This scarab was excavated from the Scarab Factory in Egypt, a site associated with the manufacture of these amulets during the Late Period, offering a glimpse into the religious and cultural significance of such objects, particularly in relation to deities like Amun and influential figures like Psamtek II.

This artifact is a mould-made scarab from the 26th Dynasty of Ancient Egypt, dating between 600-570 BC. Crafted from a glazed composition, the scarab's back is simply detailed, featuring some indication of the clypeus, with single lines marking the prothorax and elytra. The sides display legs suggested through some modelling and undercut triangular shapes. Its underside is incised with a hieroglyphic inscription, although the glaze has been lost, leaving the cream core visible. The signs, despite erosion, are still recognizable and include motifs such as a sun-disc, men-draughtboard, hes-vase on the right, and a rpt-palm frond on the left. The inscription is vertically arranged and transliterates to "Hs xnsw," meaning "Praised by Khonsu," associating the scarab with the god Khonsu. This artifact was longitudinally pierced and discovered in Naukratis, offering insights into its function and cultural significance within the context of Ancient Egypt.

This miniature scarab, originating from the 26th Dynasty in Egypt and dating between 600 and 570 BC, is a mould-made artifact crafted from a glazed composition, although the glaze appears either lost or never applied, as noted in the Egypt Exploration Fund distribution list. The back is intricately modelled with a clypeus and head, with the prothorax and elytra delineated by single lines. The underside of this very crudely made piece features an incised or possibly stamped depiction of a bird, such as a goose or duck, accompanied by a sun disc above and a potential lotus flower to the right.
